context: The G-Class traces its silhouette back to a 1979 military design that Mercedes-Benz has deliberately kept almost unchanged in appearance across four decades, even as the underlying W463 platform was fully re-engineered in 2018. In India it is sold exclusively through a handful of dealerships in petrol form, as the G 500 and the AMG-tuned G 63, with volumes so low that each unit is effectively a bespoke, allocation-based sale rather than a showroom-floor purchase.

This extreme scarcity, combined with import duties that make a new G-Class meaningfully more expensive each time prices are revised, is the main reason it depreciates far more slowly than any mass-market SUV and even most other luxury SUVs; a handful of well-documented, low-mileage examples have resold in India at or close to their original price during periods of high demand and import-cost escalation.

Unlike volume luxury SUVs, the G-Class's value is driven almost entirely by scarcity and brand cachet rather than feature depreciation or technology obsolescence, so buyers should expect resale price to track global production allocation and import-duty trends as much as the age or condition of the specific vehicle.

The used market for the G-Class in India is extremely thin, concentrated almost entirely in Mumbai and Delhi NCR, which means finding a buyer can take considerably longer than for any mainstream SUV even though the eventual price realised is high relative to depreciation elsewhere in the large SUV segment.

faq.q: What is the resale value of a Mercedes-Benz G-Class in India?
faq.a: A G-Class retains roughly 90% of its ex-showroom price after two years and about 86% after three years, still holding near 78% at year five, among the slowest depreciation curves of any vehicle sold in India as of September 2026.

faq.q: Why does the G-Class hold value so much better than other luxury SUVs?
faq.a: Its 3-year retention of about 86% is roughly 26 points above the Large SUV segment average of 60%, driven by extremely limited allocation, rising import duties on each price revision, and strong brand cachet that keeps demand ahead of the very small supply of used units.

faq.q: Is the G 63 AMG a better resale bet than the G 500?
faq.a: Both trade at similarly strong retention percentages, but the G 63 AMG's higher starting price and stronger halo status typically mean it finds a buyer faster in the thin resale market, even though percentage retention is comparable across the range.

faq.q: How much does a G-Class depreciate per year?
faq.a: A G-Class loses only about 6% of value in year one and continues at a slow 2-3 percentage point annual retention drop through year five, where it still holds roughly 78%, far flatter than any volume SUV in India.

faq.q: Which city gives the best resale price for a G-Class?
faq.a: Mumbai trades around +4% above the national mid due to the country's deepest ultra-luxury buyer pool, while Kolkata trades roughly -3% because of a very limited local market for vehicles at this price point.
